system:
You are the reading pass of an illustration engine. You read one large division of a work (a whole text such as a scripture, a novel or a story collection) and return its skeleton as JSON. The engine later draws pictures of the text's moments, so for every stretch of text it needs to know who is on stage and where, and it needs a draft brief for illustrators.

The text comes as numbered units. Each unit line starts with its id (for example `17:4` or `[12]`). Lines starting with `##` are headings, not units.

Return:

1. characters: one entry per individual (a person, a being, or an animal that acts) who appears in or is named in the text.
   - One individual is one entry, even when the text uses different names, titles or descriptions for them. List every form in `aliases`: other names, nicknames, titles, descriptions, and disguises or assumed names.
   - Different individuals who share a name or a title get separate entries, one each. Never fold two people into one entry because they share a name. When a title passes from one holder to another (a ruler dies or is succeeded, an office changes hands), the new holder is a new entry. The `note` must say in one line who this is and how to tell them apart from anyone else with the same name: whose child, spouse or servant they are, their role, and where in the text they appear.
   - A disguised, renamed or unnamed person who the text later identifies is the same entry as their named self, with the disguise or description in `aliases`. If you suspect two entries are one individual but the text does not settle it, keep both and set `same_person_as` on the less certain one to the other's id; otherwise set it to "".
   - Skip people who occur only inside a list of names (a genealogy or roster) and never act.
   - Add a group (an army, a crowd, a household) only when it acts as one on stage, with kind "group".
2. locations: one entry per place where action happens, with aliases and a one-line note. Include places the text refers to only by description ("the sea", "the valley", "the house") when the context shows which place it is, under the place's proper name if the work gives one anywhere.
3. sections: split the text into story sections, runs of consecutive units that tell one episode, the way a study edition's headings or a novel's scenes do. Start a new section when the time, the place or the main action changes. Every unit belongs to exactly one section; sections are in order, with no gaps and no overlaps. This division has 1213 units. Aim for roughly 67 sections (54 to 80), averaging about 18 units each; some sections will be much shorter and some longer. Never split one continuous scene, conversation or battle, but do split long speeches, lists, sets of instructions and law codes wherever the topic changes. Give the ids of each section's first and last unit and a short title. For each section:
   - setting: ids of the locations where its action happens.
   - on_stage: ids of every character present in the section's action, whether the section names them or only refers to them by a pronoun, a title or a description, or does not mention them but they are clearly there.
   - mentioned_only: ids of characters the section names or refers to who are not present.
4. brief: a draft brief for illustrators, for this division only. It holds only what is true across the whole division or a whole stretch of its world: one person or place is described in the cast, not here, and one episode's look belongs to its section, not here.
   - tone: one line on the mood the pictures should carry.
   - depiction_rules: a short list of how certain things in this text may or may not be shown, drawn from the text and from what you know about the work.
   - era: the stretch of the world this division is set in: a name, its people (who lives there and what they look like), dress, buildings and objects, and technology (what exists and what does not yet exist).
   Keep the brief under 200 words.

Use short, stable snake_case ids (for example `david`, `the_queen`, `main_street`). Section entries may only use ids from your own characters and locations lists. Do not quote the text.

characters.name: Moses
characters.note: Hebrew prophet and leader, raised by Pharaoh's daughter, who leads Israel out of Egypt; son of Levi's line, husband of Zipporah; appears throughout Exodus.

characters.name: Aaron
characters.note: Moses' older brother and spokesman, first high priest; son of Amram and Jochebed; appears from chapter 4 onward.

characters.name: Yahweh
characters.note: The God of Israel, who speaks from the burning bush, from the cloud and fire, and from Sinai; depicted through signs, voices and glory rather than a visible form.

characters.name: Pharaoh (the king who did not know Joseph)
characters.note: The Egyptian king of chapters 1 to 2 who enslaves Israel and orders the infants killed; died during Moses' exile.

characters.name: Pharaoh (of the plagues)
characters.note: The Egyptian king who refuses to release Israel from chapter 5 onward and pursues them to the Red Sea; a successor to the oppressor, not the same reign.

characters.name: Pharaoh's daughter
characters.note: Princess of Egypt who finds Moses in the basket among the reeds and adopts him; appears in chapter 2.

characters.name: Miriam
characters.note: Sister of Moses and Aaron who watches the basket in chapter 2 and leads the women's song at the sea in chapter 15.

characters.name: Jethro
characters.note: Priest of Midian, father of Zipporah, who gives Moses counsel on judging the people in chapter 18.

characters.name: Zipporah
characters.note: Midianite wife of Moses who circumcises their son at a lodging place in chapter 4; daughter of the priest of Midian.

characters.name: Joshua
characters.note: Moses' young servant who leads the fight against Amalek and stays at the tent; son of Nun.

characters.name: Hur
characters.note: Companion who helps hold up Moses' hands in the battle against Amalek and is left in charge at the mountain.

characters.name: Bezalel
characters.note: Master craftsman of Judah, son of Uri, who builds the tabernacle and its furnishings in chapters 31, 35 to 39.

characters.name: Oholiab
characters.note: Craftsman of Dan, son of Ahisamach, who works alongside Bezalel on the tabernacle.

characters.name: Nadab and Abihu
characters.note: Sons of Aaron who go up the mountain with the elders in chapter 24; named in the priestly lists.

characters.name: the elders of Israel
characters.note: Leaders of the people who gather with Moses and Aaron, and who go up Sinai with them in chapter 24.

characters.name: the people of Israel
characters.note: The whole company of Israel, who murmur, make the golden calf, and act together at the mountain and in the camp.

characters.name: the magicians of Egypt
characters.note: Egyptian sorcerers who imitate Aaron's signs at first and then fail at the lice.

characters.name: the Egyptian taskmasters
characters.note: Overseers who drive Israel's labor and beat their Israelite foremen.

characters.name: the Egyptian army
characters.note: Pharaoh's chariots and horsemen who pursue Israel into the sea and are drowned.

characters.name: Shiphrah and Puah
characters.note: Two Hebrew midwives who defy Pharaoh's order to kill the boy babies.

characters.name: Amalek
characters.note: Nation that attacks Israel at Rephidim; the people fought in the battle.

locations.name: Egypt
locations.note: The land of Israel's bondage and of the plagues, with its cities Pithom and Raamses, the river Nile and the palace of Pharaoh.

locations.name: Goshen
locations.note: The region in Egypt where Israel dwells, spared from the plagues.

locations.name: Midian
locations.note: Land where Moses flees and tends Jethro's flock, with the well and the mountain of God.

locations.name: Mount Sinai
locations.note: The mountain where the burning bush appears, where the covenant is given, and where the golden calf is made at its foot.

locations.name: the Red Sea
locations.note: The sea that parts for Israel and closes over the Egyptian army.

locations.name: the wilderness
locations.note: The desert between Egypt and the promised land, where Israel murmurs and receives manna and water.

locations.name: Rephidim
locations.note: Camp where Israel lacks water and fights Amalek.

locations.name: the camp
locations.note: The encampment of Israel at Sinai, where the tent of meeting and the calf are set up.

locations.name: the Tent of Meeting
locations.note: Portable sanctuary built by the craftsmen, where God meets Moses and the cloud rests.

brief.tone: Awe and wonder against oppression, drawn with restraint: dread at the plagues and the sea, and holiness in the sanctuary and on the mountain.
depiction_rules: Depict God only through signs: the burning bush, the pillar of cloud and fire, the glory on the mountain, never a visible human-like form.
Show the plagues as natural catastrophes as the text describes them, with Egypt's suffering shown plainly.
The Ten Commandments may be indicated by tablets, not by dwelling on violence in the law codes.
The golden calf and the slaying of idolaters can be shown with gravity but not gratuitous gore.
Sanctuary furnishings should follow the given pattern in gold, acacia wood, bronze and blue, purple and scarlet linen.

era.name: Late Bronze Age Egypt and the Sinai wilderness
era.people: Egyptians of the New Kingdom with shaved heads and linen kilts, Hebrew families as desert-dwelling laborers, and Midianite herders in the wilderness.
era.dress: Linen kilts and wigs for Egyptians, simple tunics and cloaks for Israelites, priests in the linen tunic, robe, ephod, breastplate and turban of the tabernacle.
era.buildings_and_objects: Brick storage cities such as Pithom and Raamses, Egyptian palaces and chariots, tents of goatskin in the wilderness, and the portable tabernacle with its acacia boards, gold overlay and bronze altar.
era.technology: Chariots, bronze and gold working, woven linen and goat-hair cloth, mud brick, and papyrus boats; no iron tools in common use and no writing beyond inscriptions and engraved stones.
